transcript.text: How is everybody doing? Primitive Nomad here, and welcome back to another Dragon
Wilds video. Progression in Dragon Wilds will feel familiar to some of you guys if you've played other survival games.
But, there are a few systems working alongside it. Progression is built around exploring new regions, finding
stronger materials, and using those materials to improve your equipment and gear. As you move farther into Ashan
fall, the regions become more dangerous, but they also give you access to the materials needed to match that region's
difficulty. Those new materials let you improve your tools, weapons, armor, and overall gear as you continue progressing
through the game. Now, materials are not the only way to progress in Dragon Wilds. Your power level, skills, and
crafting stations are a big part of your general progression. Finding a new material does not automatically mean you
can upgrade your equipment and gear. You also need the right tools to gather it, the right skill level to process and
work with those new materials, and the right crafting benches to turn those materials into useful upgrades. So, as
you move deeper into Ashan fall, your gear, tools, skills, as well as your base all need to progress with you. In
this guide, I'll break down how those systems work together, what you should pay attention to, and how progression
naturally moves from one region to the next. Now, the easiest way to understand progression is to look at the regions
themselves. As you move through Ashan fall, new regions introduce new resources. Early in the game, you'll be
working with basic materials, but as you move farther into the world, you'll start finding stronger metals, better
wood, new animal resources, plants, fiber, and unique materials dropped by enemies. Those resources are what open
the next stage of your progression. So, when you reach a new region, pay attention to what that area is giving
you. If you start seeing new ore deposits, different tree types, new creatures, or materials you haven't seen
before, start collecting them. When you collect a material for the first time, you'll normally start unlocking recipes
that use that material. A new ore, wood, a piece of leather, cloth, fiber, plant,
or enemy drop that you find around Ashan fall could be connected to a new recipe
you haven't discovered yet. Now, there's one easily missed mechanic in Dragon Wilds. Some recipes may not become
available until you bring those resources back to your base and interact with the crafting station associated
with it. So, if you pick up something new and even if you do get recipes from that new material, you still want to
bring it back to your base, have it in your inventory, and check your different crafting stations. Upon interacting with
the stations, you may find even more recipes tied to that material once you interact with the correct station. Next,
we're going to go over a gear tiers as well as your power level. Weapons, armor, and tools all move through
different tiers as you progress through Dragon Wilds. As you reach new regions and discover stronger materials, you'll
start gaining access to higher tier equipment that is better suited for the enemies and challenges of those areas.
One of the easiest ways to see where your combat equipment currently sits at is through your power level. Regions and
enemies also have their own power level, so this gives you a quick comparison between your current setup and the
content you're trying to take on. If your power level is significantly below the enemy or region you're entering,
you're going to feel a massive difference. Your attacks may feel weaker, enemies can feel much more
dangerous, and fights generally will become harder. Now, you don't need to replace every single piece of equipment
the second you walk into a new region, but your power level gives you a good indication on whether your current gear
is keeping up with your progression. Your displayed power level is based on the armor you currently have equipped.
Keep in mind if you do mix different tiers of gear, the game averages them together and rounds them down. An easy
way to understand your power level is by five different symbols. A white diamond indicates that the zone and enemies are
neutral, and this is normally found in Temple Woods. An orange diamond indicates that a player's power level is
one level below the enemy or zone. A yellow diamond indicates that the player and the enemy zone are the same power
level. A green diamond indicates that the player's power level is above the enemy zone. Keep in mind there is
another symbol and it is a diamond with a skull in it. This indicates that the player's power level is more than one
level below the enemy or zone. Now, you can still fight in those regions, but it is going to be increasingly difficult
and you usually want to stay around one level below or match the region's tier. Your gathering tools are another huge
part of progression because they determine what resources you can collect. Your pickaxe, logging axe,
shovel, and even your farming tools have their own progression alongside your weapons and armor. As you move into new
regions, you'll eventually find ore, trees, and other resources that your current tools simply aren't strong
enough to gather. That's usually your sign that you need to upgrade that tool before you can fully take advantage of
the resources in that area. This is the first thing that you should focus on when entering a region. I recommend you
upgrading your tools as your main priority. And if you do find a new resource that you can't gather yet, mark
it on your map and come back later once you've upgraded the correct tool. Now, overall, your combat gear helps with
survival in a new region, but your tools are what allow you to collect the materials needed to progress through
that region. Now, there are two other major parts of progression in Dragon Wilds and this could feel very different
from other survival titles. But, these determine what materials you can process and which recipes you'll be able to
craft. The first one is your skills and skill levels. And in my opinion, this is the most important part of progression
and is a huge part of Dragon Wilds overall. Virtually everything you do in the title is connected to a skill.
Mining, wood cutting, cooking, crafting, construction, farming, and the different combat styles all have their own
progression. Now, these skills will level naturally as you use them. Mining resources increases your mining skill,
chopping trees will improve wood cutting, and when you craft items, your related crafting skills continue
progressing. Now, as those skills level up, you unlock new recipes, perks, passive bonuses, abilities, and skill
spells. This becomes especially important as you reach new regions. Finding a higher tier material doesn't
always mean you can immediately process it or turn it into the equipment you need. You may still need the correct
skill level to work with that material, unlock new recipes, or gain access to the crafting station needed to process
it. Now, you don't need to stop everything you're doing and grind every skill as high as possible before moving
forward, but you do want your main skills to keep progressing alongside the regions you're exploring. Overall, the
great thing about Dragon Wilds is that if you're gathering new materials, crafting upgrades, cooking food,
building your base, and using the different systems in the game, all of these skills are going to naturally
continue progressing with you, and they're going to level up as you just generally play the game. Now, your next
major part is your crafting stations. These are directly tied to your skill levels. With Dragon Wilds being a
survival crafting game, your base is going to be your hub where everything you've gathered throughout Aethelfall
gets processed and turned into advanced materials and resources used for higher tier recipes. As your skills increase
and you discover better materials, you'll unlock new crafting stations along with upgrades for stations you
already have. A good example is leatherworking. Early on, you can use the tannery to process basic hides into
leather. As your progression and the skills associated with it increase, you can add a buildable called the tanner's
kit. This is going to expand what the tannery can process and allows you to start working with more advanced leather
types. Later in the game, stronger materials actually require the advanced tannery. So, finding a better hide is
only the beginning when it comes to things you can craft. You still need the skill progression and the right crafting
station to turn that material into something useful. This same idea applies across the rest of your stations. Your
blacksmith bench handles many of your weapons and tools. Your armor bench handles your armor progression. Your
fletching bench handles range weapons and ammunition. And other stations are used for things like cloth, food,
potions, runes, and the other resources you'll collect throughout the game. Now,
this is why I wouldn't neglect your base or your crafting skills while progressing through the story. You may
reach a new region and find all the materials you need, but without the correct skills and crafting stations,
you won't be able to fully use them. The regions, materials, skills, and base are all meant to progress alongside each
other. And that's one of the great things about Dragon wilds. As a survival crafting title, your base is actually a
very, very important tool and hub in the progression and how you approach playing
the game. Now, I do want to mention two other general tips for you when it comes to progression. Another part of
equipment in Dragon wilds comes from something called vestiges. The normal materials you find throughout the world
give you a general path for upgrading your equipment, but vestiges can unlock additional weapons, armor, tools, and
other useful recipes. These can give you additional gear options beyond the normal equipment you unlock from simply
progressing through material tiers. This is Dragon wilds end game pieces of gear. Now, you don't need every vestige item
in order to move forward through the regions, but they can give you access to really useful equipment options for how
you want to build your character. Now, this one's pretty simple. The main story gives you a general direction through
Ashenfall. Your progression isn't only about following the next quest marker. As you explore, you should also be
opening chest, clearing vaults around Ashenfall, completing side quests, collecting vestiges, and gathering the
resources around you. A lot of your progression happens naturally through exploration. So, if a quest suddenly
takes you into a region where everything feels dramatically harder, you don't always need to brute force your way
through it. So, overall, progression in Dragon wilds is really all of these systems working together. New regions
give you access to better resources. Your tools determine which of those resources you can gather. Your skills

ahead. You don't need to rush through any of it. Explore, gather the new materials you find, keep your tools and
